title: UNH English professor emeritus Andy Merton releases new autobiography - The New Hampshire
content: On Thursday Nov. 5 at 5pm, former University of New Hampshire (UNH) English professor Andy Merton is set to read passages from his new autobiography, Gloria Steinem Blurbed Me (And Other Miracles). The reading, located in Hamilton Smith Hall, brings Merton back to the place he taught writing for more than forty years. Throughout his decades at UNH, Merton taught courses ranging in subject matter from creative nonfiction, to travel writing, to advanced essay writing—all to both undergraduate and graduate students—but his main passion and role in the English Department was as a leading professor in journalism. Five years after beginning his professional career in the world of journalism through his work with various daily newspapers, such as The Gloucester Daily Times and the Boston Herald Traveler, Merton was hired by UNH to teach about the craft. However, his story at the school didn’t begin there. Merton studied as an undergraduate at UNH—graduating in 1967 with a Bachelor of Arts in History, alongside a minor in Psychology. He recollects in our interview: “ I studied journalism with the only journalist on the faculty at that time, Don Murray.” He goes on to say that, as a professor years down the line, he worked with Murray to expand course offerings, helping to pave the way for the richly diverse English Department the university is proud of today. Between 2008-2014, Merton was the chair of UNH’s English Department. During his forty-three years as an integral part of the school’s faculty, Merton’s love of writing not only blossomed, but expanded into new territory, thanks in part to the “influences of [his] English Department poet colleagues, Charles Simic and Mekeel McBride.” In 1985, Merton’s affinity for the genre deepened, eventually making its way into both his creative writing and coursework. Merton would go on to have four of his poetry books published and an opportunity to teach poetry writing workshops in his last few years as an English professor. Poetry and journalism acted as guiding forces in Merton’s life, culminating in his autobiography, Gloria Steinem Blurbed Me (And Other Miracles), which hit shelves this past summer. Merton details how the book came together. He claims that it was “not the book [he] started out to write,” an original vision he described to be a memoir “purely about [his] women’s rights and gay rights activism,” but through writing and continually getting off track telling “other stories,” the book flourished into something else entirely. His “memoir became [his] autobiography.” From his early childhood in a Jewish family following WWII, to his college days at UNH (which, in fact, includes his writing for The New Hampshire), to his writing career as a professor, journalist and, eventually, a poet, “Gloria covers most of [Merton’s] life.” In many respects, the form of his work directly relates to his story, in that he “uses poetry as part of the narrative,” a facet of the book he ensured would be accessible enough so that readers who may not be familiar with much poetry, or perhaps simply don’t enjoy it, can engage with the novel in meaningful ways. “The poems are designed to move the text along,” Merton explains. In broad ways, Gloria was a synthesis of Merton’s professional and creative life. It’s a story steeped in realism that is told, in part, with poetry. Merton mentioned that his process for writing the book balanced his journalistic intuitions with those of poetry and creative writing. Being used to rigid deadlines in the world of journalism, Merton made sure to write “200 words a day,” a self-imposed rule that he made sure his editor enforced. Still, his expedition in lifelong reflection was a joyous one—full of memories, conversations with friends, digging through archived published work, and “small ‘oh, yeah!’ moments almost every day.” Gloria Steinem Blurbed Me (And Other Miracles) was published on Aug. 15 by Accents Publishing, a small, independent press that mostly publishes poetry books—including some of Merton’s own. It’s a book that celebrates a life in pursuit of what the author truly loves: the craft of writing and the transferral of that craft to the next generations of writers. “My career at UNH was a dream job, allowing me to combine teaching—which I thoroughly enjoyed—with my writing,” he proudly says. Following a few months’ worth of readings and occasional podcast appearances, Merton is returning to UNH to read passages from his autobiography. The reading will take place in Hamilton Smith Hall on Thursday, Nov. 5 at 5pm—showcasing a writer with a deep devotion to the art, speaking in the very place that inspired him for more than four decades. Alex Hankins is a writer who covers stories ranging from the arts to updates within UNH's English Department. He is a graduate student in UNH's English MFA program, and received his undergraduate degree at here at UNH as well. Alex also serves as the editor for contributor writers in The New Hampshire.

title: UNH students, faculty oppose potential removal of up to 300k books from library - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: Justin Kostopulos is not a traditional art history student at UNH. He’s 35 and a commuter, so he spends a lot of his time between classes wandering the stacks of the library. When he found out the Dimond Library was reviewing nearly 300,000 print titles for potential removal, he started a petition to ask the university to reconsider. Within a week, it gathered over 600 signatures. “Removing these texts, I think, erases decades of accrued wisdom and insight,” he said. “It deprives students the unique experience of just handling a physical book, which many times can spark curiosity and critical thinking in ways that digital media often cannot.” The book review is part of an effort by UNH to modernize its library, which was last renovated in 1996. UNH said in internal communications to staff and students that was shared with NHPR that the school was a decade overdue in going through their collections. UNH is also planning to open a new student center in the library’s unused space in a few years. UNH said their library is prioritizing digital collections to serve online students, but Kostopulos said there’s still a lot of value to keeping physical copies. “After speaking with many of my peers since starting this petition,” he said. “Many students, myself included, retain information better through physical books rather than reading something online.” The university gave faculty six weeks to review the list of potential titles, ending on Oct. 21. But some faculty, including UNH History Professor Eliga Gould, said that wasn’t enough time. As a historian, Gould also said that interests and access to technology often change, and it’s valuable to keep books, especially older ones. “There is also no guarantee that books now available in online databases always will be there,” he said. “Some of the books slated for removal are over 100 years old. Will a pdf still be here in another 100 years? Today's best practice is all too often tomorrow's regret.” He also recalled what some faculty members jokingly called “dumpstergate,” when thousands of books from the Dimond Library were found in a dumpster in 2014. Even though the online collections may be more convenient, Gould said there is value to keeping print books, especially in a public university, since online books are not accessible to a general public that doesn’t have login to large online collections like HathiTrust. “It's hugely important to have those print books available,” he said. “We're a public institution. This is open to the general public and that's a huge part of our mission as a land grant university.” The university is still planning on moving forward with the renovation, but released a FAQ internally to address concerns. The FAQ said the books were selected for review because they hadn’t been checked out in over a decade, and are easily found in another library, or online. “We default to purchasing electronic books rather than print books. We don’t have the budget to purchase more than one copy of a book, so the collection growth is all electronic and has been for the last ten years, since we adopted an e-preferred policy,” the FAQ said. “The print books we own are an increasingly aging and increasingly smaller percentage of our overall collection.” The university is currently reviewing the feedback from faculty, according to the FAQ shared with staff and students. title: Turning Point USA at UNH hosts a 'Pick Up the Mic' with Jack Posobiec - The New Hampshire
content: On Thursday, Oct. 22 Turning Point USA (TPUSA) hosted a surprise Pick Up The Mic event at the University of New Hampshire (UNH) featuring right-wing political figure Jack Posobiec, popular on the social media platform X, debating abortion rights, foreign policy, religion and more with students. The event was located on the Great Lawn from 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM and attracted around 200 attendees. Among the organizers were Caleb Brower, sophomore and chapter president of TPUSA at UNH. Brower expressed that the event was much more successful than anyone had anticipated, considering the lack of political activity at UNH and the size of the Chapter on-campus. Brower’s only critique was the majority of the attendee’s preaching to the choir. “Unfortunately most people agreed,” said Brower. These attendees explained that they did not feel comfortable speaking on their political views in class and expressed gratitude towards the event. There were one or two people that were not interested in civil discourse and approached with hostility. “They start yelling ‘you shouldn't be here.’” Posebiec said during an interview. “And it seemed to me though that they seem to think that if you have a conversation about something where people disagree, that even the civil exhibit of that is somehow problematic.” Brower similarly criticized these interactions as they only produced “one-liners” trying to win the last word instead of productive debates. Brower recalled that foreign policy was the most touched on subject and was surprised by its popularity. Specifically, the concerns were centered around tensions in the Middle East, including the U.S.’s close relationship with Israel. Folks that were left-leaning argued that the “U.S. should not be funding a genocide,” primarily referring to the war in Gaza. Additionally, right-leaning participants dissented the U.S.’s involvement with foreign countries saying that sending resources that are not mutually beneficial is not putting America first. Brower then highlighted the last question from an attendee asking about the truth of Charlie Kirk’s assassination in Sept. 2025, in light of recent theories on social media that the assasination was a conspiracy by Israel. Posobiec denied these accusations and claimed he was certain the assassination was not a larger conspiracy. No matter how controversial or problematic the question may be, Turning Point’s doctrine is committed to defending the right to free speech. Brower admired this dedication to free speech as members from Turning Point’s Headquarters in Phoenix, AZ allowed the attendee to ask questions regarding Kirk’s assassination despite already being out of time. The TPUSA Chapter at UNH has been on more people's radars than last year thanks to events such as Pick Up The Mic. Most of the executive team from previous years stepped down, leading to Brower stepping up as president and taking agency in this role. “[The chapter] Really didn't exist in a meaningful way beforehand,” said Brower. Brower ran into a learning curve as he ambitiously took on a leading role without guidance. A main challenge was not becoming a “repeat” of the republican party club at UNH. To combat this, Brower focused on events rather than weekly meetings with the TPUSA chapter. During UNH’s Parents Weekend on Oct. 17, TPUSA’s chapter set up their own tailgate with free food, games and invited local republican politicians. Brower said this was “certainly the move” as just these two events have attracted great success for TPUSA at UNH. Brower’s motivation is relentless despite UNH’s lack of political presence. TPUSA plans to host at least one more major event this semester and Brower wants to make sure it is memorable. The struggle Brower faces is choosing from a TPUSA’s list of political figures, as many are irrelevant to the average person. “We’re gonna go all out and get someone who [people] actually care about,” said Brower. As the first major US health insurer to report each season, its results are viewed as a guide for the wider sector, and readers following US Healthcare Stocks paid close attention to what it said about medical costs. The message was encouraging. After a period of elevated medical spending and operational challenges, the company showed clear progress in restoring margins, even though total revenue was slightly lower than a year earlier as it deliberately shed less profitable membership. The medical care ratio measures how much of each premium dollar is spent on patient care. A lower ratio means more is left over for operating costs and profit. UnitedHealth's ratio improved compared with the same quarter last year and came in better than analysts expected. Management credited improved medical cost management, better alignment of benefits and pricing, and enhancements in care delivery. The figure also included a benefit from reserve releases for earlier claims, which flattered the result. Investors therefore separated the one-time reserve effect from underlying improvement when judging the quarter. Not every line improved. Executives said commercial medical cost trends are still running above the company's initial assumptions, driven by specialty drugs, higher clinician costs and arbitration disputes over surprise billing. They described the trend as stabilising rather than accelerating, but it pushes out the timeline for long-term commercial margin targets. Optum Health, the care delivery business that struggled last year, showed a sharp improvement in operating earnings. The rebound reflects renewed focus on value-based care, tighter clinical programmes and operational changes, including exiting markets that lacked sufficient infrastructure to support profitable care. Online self-scheduling and home health visits both increased, showing how the business is shifting toward more efficient and convenient care models. AI tools that summarise medical records are also reducing administrative time for physicians. The operating cost ratio fell from a year earlier, reflecting investments to modernise operations and streamline administrative processes. Lower overhead allows more of each revenue dollar to reach profit, complementing improvements in the medical care ratio. Cash flow from operations was healthy and comfortably exceeded net income, supporting the company's financial flexibility as it continues its recovery plan. UnitedHealthcare served fewer people than a year earlier, partly because employers moved coverage elsewhere and partly because the company pulled back from unprofitable plans. Management signalled that Medicare Advantage margins should end the year near the upper end of their target range. Medicaid performance also improved, with the company working with states to close gaps between reimbursement rates and medical costs. These efforts reflect a broader focus on profitable growth rather than membership volume. The raised outlook exceeded analyst expectations. Management reaffirmed confidence in sustainable growth next year within its long-term target range and said analyst forecasts for next year look conservative. A full outlook for next year is expected before year-end. That comment matters because it suggests the recovery has momentum. However, the floor implied for the fourth quarter is modest, reflecting caution in a business where costs can shift quickly. Medical cost trends remain the biggest swing factor. Regulatory issues, including Medicare rate decisions, Medicaid funding, quality star ratings and an ongoing federal investigation, also carry uncertainty. Political debates about healthcare costs may influence the operating environment. Employer membership losses may continue if competitors offer lower prices. Balancing growth and margins will remain a central challenge for management. UnitedHealth is using technology to reduce administrative friction for patients and doctors. Changes to prior authorisation processes, faster claims handling and digital tools for scheduling are meant to lower costs and improve the experience. These efforts also respond to public and political pressure to simplify healthcare. The company's pharmacy services business remains another important profit contributor, though drug pricing reform and scrutiny of pharmacy benefit managers continue to shape its outlook. As a large member of the NYSE Composite, UnitedHealth's results set the tone for health insurance stocks. This quarter showed that disciplined pricing and cost management can restore profitability even when revenue growth is flat. The upcoming outlook for next year will be the next major catalyst. Investors will want proof that earnings can grow even while enrolment stays flat, confirming that the recovery is durable rather than temporary. The broader industry is watching as well. Other insurers face similar cost pressures, and UnitedHealth's progress suggests that pricing actions and benefit changes taken over the past year are starting to restore balance across the sector. title: UNH Students Nominated for Marshall, Rhodes Scholarships - University of New Hampshire
content: UNH students Will Steere ’27 and Eben Quenneville ’27 were nominated for 2026 Marshall scholarships, with Quenneville also earning an endorsement for a 2026 Rhodes scholarship. Marshall and Rhodes scholarships are two of the most prestigious and competitive awards available to U.S. students. Steere learned this week that he is a finalist for the Marshall opportunity and will have an interview upcoming. Quenneville was not selected as a finalist for either honor. The Rhodes scholarship provides support for students to study at the University of Oxford and is the “oldest and most celebrated” international postgraduate award, according to the Rhodes website. Marshall scholarships offer 1-to-3 years of post-graduate study to students pursuing a graduate degree in the United Kingdom. Recipients can study in virtually any field at a UK institution of their choice. “Being nominated by UNH for the Marshall Scholarship is an exciting recognition for progressing toward this national award. It feels special to have passed the interview process and earned a nomination by UNH, and I am hopeful that I can win this scholarship and bring recognition to UNH and CEPS,” Steere says. Adds Quenneville: “It's an extraordinary privilege to have so many wonderful mentors at UNH and beyond. When I arrived at UNH, I certainly wasn't imagining that I would one day be applying for scholarships like the Rhodes and Marshall. But over the past few years, I've had opportunities to contribute to exciting scientific research, help launch a satellite, work with researchers around the world, and make a meaningful difference in physics education on campus. Those experiences, and the encouragement of the people I've worked with, have given me the confidence to pursue opportunities that once seemed out of reach.” Steere, a chemical engineering honors student, earned first place for his presentation on catalytic biomass valorization research at UNH’s Undergraduate Research Conference during his junior year, an achievement he includes among his proudest as a student. He also earned an internship at the National Laboratory of the Rockies in Golden, Colorado, which he described as “one of the most impactful experiences I have had.” “I connected with top researchers in my field and learned about the operations of the US Department of Energy, but I also led a high-level research project tied to the Genesis mission aiming to make progress toward AI-driven research laboratories for catalysis,” Steere says. Steere hopes to earn a Ph.D. in chemical engineering “to transfer my research in catalysis into impactful commercial processes.” He is interested in founding a startup based off the catalytic technology he plans to develop during his Ph.D. work or in joining a research institute like a national laboratory in the United States or somewhere global. Quenneville, an engineering physics honors student, counts his work improving physics education for other students at UNH among his proudest achievements since arriving on campus. He has been involved in the Physics Learning Assistant program since his first semester, an offering that places undergraduates in introductory physics classrooms to help their peers work through problems and overcome conceptual hurdles, he says. “It’s tremendously rewarding to help other students develop their understanding of physics,” Quenneville says. “Teaching also forces you to understand the material more deeply yourself, and I think that experience has been invaluable to my own success in research and advanced coursework.” He has also worked with Alec Mercer ’26 and Benjamin Chandran, professor in the College of Engineering and Physical Sciences, to overhaul UNH’s physics tutoring center, now known as the Physics Assistance and Resource Center (PARC). Quenneville has pursued a variety of research as a student (he earned the Barry Goldwater scholarship in recognition of that research), most recently partnering with Chandran and Jonathan Squire from the University of Otago in New Zealand to better understand solar wind. He also helped develop and launch 3UCubed, a satellite “about the size of a loaf of bread” that was part of NASA’s IMAP student collaboration. Quenneville’s career goal is to become a professor of plasma physics, a pursuit “that would allow me to combine my two great interests: teaching and research.” He credited the “wonderful people” at UNH’s Office of National Fellowships, who have played a key role in facilitating the Marshall and Rhodes opportunities as well as a host of others throughout his time at UNH, including the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship and a Fulbright. title: UNH Hosts New England’s First Aerospace Industry Expo - University of New Hampshire
content: New England’s aerospace industry took center stage at the University of New Hampshire on October 28 and 29 as the university hosted the region’s first comprehensive space-focused expo, bringing together innovators, researchers, manufacturers, government leaders and the next generation of talent for two days of discovery, collaboration and inspiration. Presented in partnership with the N.H. Department of Business and Economic Affairs (BEA) and the NH Aerospace & Defense Consortium (NHADC), the inaugural Northeast Space, Technology, Trade, and Research Expo (NE STTAR Expo) transformed UNH’s Memorial Union Building into a hub of cutting-edge technology, groundbreaking research, and industry engagement. More than 700 attendees learned about emerging technologies, research innovations and workforce opportunities across aerospace, autonomous systems, propulsion, advanced manufacturing, and materials science. “The aerospace industry is vital to New Hampshire’s economy, supporting good-paying jobs and businesses across the Granite State as our leading export industry,” said U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who attended the event. “It is thanks to everyone who joined us at the inaugural NE STTAR Expo, especially the University of New Hampshire, the New Hampshire Department of Business and Economic Affairs and the New Hampshire Aerospace & Defense Consortium, for the partnerships you all foster between industry, academia and government to ensure we remain on the cutting-edge and a global leader.” The Expo featured 64 exhibitors, including 50 businesses and 14 university and partner organizations. Approximately 450 industry professionals, exhibitors and other attendees participated, along with 175 students in grades 8-12 and 80 UNH students. The Expo also offered tours of the Space Science Center in Morse Hall and the John Olson Advanced Manufacturing Center throughout both days. The event highlighted the growing importance of New Hampshire’s aerospace and defense sector, which includes roughly 300 companies, employs more than 10,500 people, and generates an estimated $7.5 billion in economic output statewide. As a national leader in space research, UNH provided a fitting venue for the event. The university’s work spans mission leadership, instrument development, data analysis, and simulation, with research ranging from Earth’s upper atmosphere to the farthest reaches of the universe. The first day focused on industry engagement through keynote presentations, technology demonstrations, exhibits, and networking opportunities. The second day shifted attention to workforce development, connecting students with professionals through a career fair, educational programming, and campus facility tours. The inaugural expo underscored New Hampshire’s growing role in the aerospace and space economy while fostering partnerships that will help drive future innovation and workforce development. “As we look ahead, we want more New Hampshire companies to see UNH as a resource they can turn to for research, equipment, and highly skilled graduates,” said UNH President Elizabeth Chilton. “And we want more students to have the opportunity to apply what they’re learning alongside the businesses that are helping shape the future of this industry.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Williamson Hall is closing for renovations, and that means changes are coming to the UNH student community - The New Hampshire
content: The dormitory hall that decades of students have loved and called home has been announced to close next year for renovations, causing pending questions left unanswered about what this means for not only the incoming freshmen but for the students already living on campus. “Williamson construction will begin in June 2027. It will reopen in time for Fall 2028. Christensen will begin in May 2028, with completion for students coming in Fall 2029,” said Executive Director of Media Relations Tania DeLuzuriaga. An email sent out from UNH Housing and Residential Life on September 21, 2026, detailed that Williamson Hall will undergo renovations during the 2027-2028 academic year. After those renovations are completed, Christensen Hall will undergo its own renovations during the 2028-2029 academic year. However, many students were left confused by the email. “Details of the project and what it will entail will be available at a later date,” said UNH Housing and Residential Life via email. Williamson Hall houses approximately 424 students, primarily first-years. The residential hall is described as “the host to our First Year Experience with programs and events geared to new Wildcats so you can get the most out of UNH,” on UNH Housing and Residential Life’s website. UNH’s policy states that Freshmen and Sophomores must live on campus for their first four semesters, unless they are over 21 years old. So, what does closing down one of the biggest homes to first-years look like for the rest of campus? According to UNH, based on university enrollment and housing projections, while Williamson is closed, Hitchcock and Hubbard Hall will become first-year student-only communities. “The way Hitchcock and Hubbard [residential halls] are set up is good for first-year communities,” Assistant Director of Housing, Jeremy Homolka, said. “In Hitchcock, we liked the gendered floors for first-year students because it's similar to how Williamson is structured.” Returning students will not be able to choose from Hitchcock and Hubbard; however, current residents will have a special selection day that gives them the chance to choose from the remaining residence halls across campus. “Students who are living in Hitchcock and Hubbard did not know they wouldn't be able to live there next year,” Homolka said. “We are giving them their own little phase where they get their pick first from communities across campus, so they’re taking priority.” Renovations within Williamson and Christenson will include upgraded, modernized bathrooms, and will not stop at the two first-year residential halls. “We’re doing this not to alter the experiences students have,” Director of Residential Life, Katie Bartholomew, said. “We want to keep all of the special, wonderful connections people make in the first year, but we really need to improve the facilities there, like plumbing and heating, to provide a more modern college experience.” Housing and Residential Life made it clear that their goal is to improve the student experience with this renovation. These goals are also in line with President Chilton’s plan to transform UNH into a first-choice destination. “We hope it's the first phase in continuing to reinvest in our buildings. We're watching the enrollment in the area and making sure our building portfolio matches incoming and current students for housing,” Associate Director of Housing and Facilities, Bill Meehan, said. “We want to keep it [residential halls] safe and functional for many more years to come.”

title: America’s Most Popular GOP Governor Holds On Despite Blue Tsunami - Newsweek
content: Republican Phil Scott won another term as Vermont governor on Tuesday, defying a Democratic blue wave that swept across much of the country and reinforcing his status as one of the nation's most popular and politically resilient GOP governors. Scott won 52.6 percent of the vote against his opponent Democrat Amanda Janoo's 45.6 percent, with 99 percent of votes tallied, making this one of his toughest re-elections yet. This is now Scott's sixth successful campaign for the Vermont governor's mansion. He managed to retain his position despite an overwhelming blue wave that saw Democrats flipping many U.S. Senate, House, and gubernatorial seats, including in traditionally Republican states such as Texas and Ohio. While Janoo carried the Democratic strongholds of Burlington and Montpelier, Scott ran up margins across much of the rest of Vermont, allowing the Republican governor to once again assemble a broad statewide coalition. The results come shortly after a new University of New Hampshire (UNH) Green Mountain State Poll, released Sunday, found Janoo leading the Republican incumbent 51 percent to 43 percent among likely voters, including those leaning toward a candidate. Independent Brian Judd had 4 percent. “Republican Governor Phil Scott has comfortably won re-election in recent years, but he trails Democrat Amanda Janoo in the final days of the 2026 campaign,” the poll’s press release said. UNH is the only pollster that had shown Janoo ahead in the general election, and the most recent competing survey, from State Navigate, had Scott up 3 points last week (49 percent to 46 percent). “We started this campaign with a goal of building a movement of Vermonters who love this state,” Janoo said in a statement to Newsweek reacting to the poll. “Vermonters who may not share the same backgrounds or lived experiences, but who believe we can do more for each other and for our state than sit on the sidelines when things get hard.” Newsweek reached out to Scott's campaign for comment. In Morning Consult's most recent state rankings, based on surveys of registered voters from April 1 through June 30, Scott had a net approval rating of +52, the highest of any governor. North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong followed at +50 and Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon at +49. A Morning Consult ranking released in February put his approval at 74 percent, with 19 percent disapproving, and listed him as the most popular governor for the 14th consecutive quarter. Vermont Public found his approval at 45 percent this fall, down 15 points from 2022. UNH had him at 47 percent approving and 47 percent disapproving in September. State Navigate's poll showed that Scott had 58 percent approval. Scott has said this is his toughest race since he first won in 2016, and he has pinned much of that on Democratic enthusiasm. Scott’s number has barely changed in UNH’s polling this year. He had 42 percent in June, 44 percent in July and 43 percent in both September and October. Janoo, however, has climbed over the same period, going from 27 percent to 33 percent, then 49 percent and now 51 percent, the first UNH figure to count leaners. The partisan breakdown shows why. Janoo wins 78 percent of Democrats, up from 73 percent in September, while 20 percent stick with Scott. Scott holds 85 percent of Republicans, with 10 percent going to Judd, and carries independents 51 percent to 39 percent. He wins 25 percent of former Vice President Kamala Harris voters, while 38 percent of Janoo's supporters say they voted for Scott in 2024. The poll also found that Janoo, a 39-year-old economist who has never held office, was viewed favorably by 54 percent of likely voters and unfavorably by 29 percent. Scott’s numbers were 42 percent and 40 percent. Sean McKinley, the UNH Survey Center’s project director, told Newsweek in September that Scott had “a bit of a hill to climb.” Democratic leaders had originally hoped for a more established candidate. The party tried to recruit Attorney General Charity Clark, Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas and Treasurer Mike Pieciak to take on Scott, but all three decided to seek reelection to their current offices. Money tops the list. Asked to name their most important issue, likely voters in the UNH poll most often cited affordability or inflation, at 17 percent, followed by economic health or financial security and the tax burden or public spending, at 10 percent each. The candidates have split sharply on how to deal with them. Janoo has proposed higher taxes on top earners and universal primary care, a plan Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent, backed at a Winooski event last month. Scott argues the state has too few wealthy residents to carry that load. "One person makes a billion dollars, and when that's gone, that's gone," he said at an October 21 debate. Education is another dividing line, with Janoo opposing the forced school mergers she says Scott's overhaul would bring. AI data centers have also surfaced as Scott vetoed a bill regulating them in May, while Janoo supports a moratorium. The State Navigate survey of 1,752 likely voters, conducted October 23-25, had Scott ahead 49 percent to 46 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.3 percentage points. Its early October poll showed him up 46 percent to 43 percent. State Navigate also found Scott keeping 66 percent of his 2024 voters while 30 percent moved to Janoo. He won 25 percent of Democrats, a bigger share than UNH found, and his job approval stood at 58 percent, with 40 percent disapproving. A Vermont Public poll conducted September 10-21 gave Scott his widest lead, 44 percent to 34 percent among likely voters, with 16 percent undecided. Scott's campaign has fought the UNH numbers since September, when campaign manager Dustin Degree called that month's poll "statistical malpractice" and pointed to a sample with far more Democrats than Republicans. The center's final 2024 poll had Scott winning 65 percent to 26 percent. He won 73.4 percent to 21.8 percent. Andrew Smith, the center's director, defended its methods at the time while acknowledging it had underestimated Scott's margin. UNH says its data were weighted in part to 2024 election results, and its October sample was 60 percent Democrats, 29 percent Republicans and 11 percent independents. The Cook Political Report moved the race from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican" last month. Sabato's Crystal Ball and Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin have it at "Lean Republican." Polymarket and Kalshi both gave Scott about a 68 percent chance of winning on Monday. Republicans face a difficult final week nationally ahead of the midterms. A Reuters/Ipsos poll of likely voters had Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot 53 percent to 44 percent, while an NPR/PBS News/Marist poll had them up 52 percent to 44 percent, with Trump's approval at 40 percent and his disapproval at 59 percent. Trump is far weaker in Vermont, where UNH put him at 20 percent approval and 77 percent disapproval. Democrats there are also more engaged, with 69 percent saying they are extremely interested in the election, compared with 59 percent of Republicans. Scott has opposed the White House on tariffs and National Guard deployments, among other issues. Nearly 140,000 Vermonters had turned in ballots by Friday morning, according to the Vermont Secretary of State's Office. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anthony Murray and Jason Lemon.

title: Jackson, LePage, and Pingree lead in final polls - WABI
content: BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Two new polls released Sunday give insight into Maine voters’ closing thoughts just days before election day. A New York Times/Press Herald/Siena poll shows democrat Troy Jackson leading incumbent senator Susan Collins by 6 points. Jackson garnered the support of 51% of the 714 likely Maine voters surveyed, while Collins was backed by 45% of participants. The margin of error for the NYT poll is 4.3%. In September’s iteration of that same poll, Collins led Jackson by 3%, showing a 9 point change in the new poll which was conducted between Oct. 27 and Nov. 1. The University of New Hampshire’s Pine Tree State Poll, conducted between Oct. 27 and Oct 31, shows Jackson sitting at 54% and Collins at 45%, though the majority of voters surveyed say they still expect Collins to win. It widens Jackson’s 4-point lead from UNH’s September poll. 87% of Jackson voters said their vote was to oppose President Donald Trump, while 66% of Collins supporters said their vote was unrelated to the president. Over 1,700 Maine residents completed the survey for UNH, 802 of which reside in Congressional District 2, and 843 residing in Congressional District 1. Their margin of error for the UNH poll is 2.4%. In the gubernatorial race, democrat Hannah Pingree leads with 49% of surveyed voters saying they plan to back her in the NYT/Press Herald/Siena poll. Republican candidate Bobby Charles trails at 37% and independent Rick Bennett at 8%. A recent Marist poll showed a much tighter race, with Charles and Pingree tied at 44%. UNH’s Survey Center says Pingree also pulled out on top in the Pine Tree State Poll. 51% or likely voters said they have or will vote for Pingree, while 40% of favored Charles and 7% said they will vote or have voted for Bennett. The Pine Tree Poll also showed 61% of those surveyed think Pingree with win, made up of 91% of Pingree supporters, 93% of Bennett supporters, and 22% of Charles supporters. 60% Charles supporters said they believe Charles will win. In the race for Maine’s second congressional district, republican former Gov. Paul LePage pulled out ahead of Democratic Maine state auditor and former secretary of state Matt Dunlap in the UNH Pine Tree State Poll, with 52% of support compared to Dunlap’s to 47%. In UNH’s September poll, Dunlap had a lead over LePage, 51% to 45%. The NYT/Press Herald/Siena poll did not conduct separate polls for each congressional district, instead asking residents which party they would vote for. 55% of voters said they would vote for the democratic candidate for congress, and 42% said they would vote for the republican candidate. In the Pine Tree State Poll, the UNH Survey Center says incumbent democrat Chellie Pingree garnered the support of 65% of voters surveyed, with republican Ronald Russell was backed by 32%. In September, Pingree was up 57% to Russell’s 35%.

title: Janoo Leads UNH’s Final Poll While Most of Its Respondents Expect Scott to Win - Compass Vermont
content: “Democratic newcomer Amanda Janoo holds a small lead over Republican incumbent Phil Scott in the race for Governor of Vermont. However, most likely voters in Vermont expect Scott to win.” That’s how the University of New Hampshire opened its final poll of the governor’s race, released Sunday. The poll has Janoo, a Democrat/Progressive, leading Scott 51% to 43% among likely voters. Janoo’s campaign emphasized that lead in a Monday release headlined “Janoo is Up Eight Points in Final Poll as Lead Over Five-Term Governor Grows.” But the same survey produced another striking finding. Sixty-two percent of likely voters expect Scott to win, while only 25% expect Janoo to. Even among Janoo’s supporters, 40% expect Scott to prevail. The poll tells two different stories: whom voters prefer, and whom they expect to win Tuesday. Pollsters usually lead by asking people whom they’ll vote for. The UNH poll also asked: “Regardless of your vote, which candidate do you think is most likely to win the 2026 election for governor?” A voter can support Janoo and still expect Scott to win. The first answer measures that voter’s own choice; the second measures that voter’s read of everyone else. And 62% expecting Scott to win is not a 62% chance that he will. The expectation question has a strong record. Economists David Rothschild and Justin Wolfers found that asking voters who will win forecast presidential elections more accurately than asking how they’ll vote. In an analysis of the 2014 elections, expectation questions missed half as many governor’s races as vote questions did. The researchers’ explanation is that people answering about expectations draw on what they know of their friends’ and family’s plans. That record gives voters’ expectations weight, but it doesn’t establish which question will prove more accurate in Vermont this year. In the UNH poll, the two questions point in opposite directions. In September, UNH had Janoo at 49% and Scott at 43%, with 6% undecided. This time, UNH added a follow-up question for undecided voters asking which way they lean. Those voters are called leaners. The 51%-to-43% figure includes them. UNH also reports the result without leaners, which is the version that matches September: Janoo 50%, Scott 42%. Janoo’s reported lead widened from six points to eight. In those directly comparable results, her support rose one point and Scott’s fell one point. Changes that small don’t, by themselves, establish that the electorate shifted. The undecided share fell from 6% to 2%. Over the same period, independent Brian Judd rose from 2% to 4%, and Freedom and Unity candidate Dean Roy picked up 1%. UNH’s bar chart is titled “With Leaners” over both its September and October panels. The September numbers didn’t include leaners. A footnote under the chart says so. UNH lists a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 points for likely voters. That figure applies to each candidate’s share, not to the gap between them. Pollsters adjust their raw results so the people who answered look like the state as a whole. That’s called weighting. A rough calculation that leaves out weighting puts the margin of error on the gap at about 5.5 points, and Janoo’s eight-point lead exceeds that estimate. But UNH says its published margins have not been adjusted for the uncertainty weighting adds. So the 5.5-point calculation doesn’t settle how precise the weighted result is. UNH’s headline on the Vermont poll reads “Blue Wave Lifts Janoo Over Scott in Vermont?” That suggests party is the reason for Janoo’s lead. The survey doesn’t establish that. Most of her supporters, 72%, say their vote is more for Janoo than against Scott, and 82% of those say it’s about her specifically. That doesn’t rule out a broader partisan pull, but it isn’t evidence of one either. UNH released its New Hampshire poll the same day under a plain headline: “Dems Lead in Federal Races, Governors Race Deadlocked.” Of the three pollsters in this story, UNH is the only one whose fall surveys have put Janoo ahead. State Navigate, Oct. 23–25, 1,752 likely voters: Scott 49%, Janoo 46%. Vermont Public, September: Scott ahead by 10 points. UNH’s final poll in 2024 had Scott 39 points ahead of Esther Charlestin. He won by nearly 52, about 13 points more than the poll showed. As Compass reported in September, polls and prediction markets have each missed in Vermont before, and neither decides the race. UNH’s poll draws from a panel of about 2,700 Vermont adults recruited at random by phone, text and mail. In September, Survey Center director Andrew Smith said that kind of panel is the same method used by Gallup, CNN and Pew. UNH weighted the sample by age, sex, education and region, and to Vermont’s 2024 election results. The sample’s recalled 2024 presidential vote, Harris 62% and Trump 31%, closely matches the actual result of 64% to 32%. The poll also finds conditions that favor a challenger this year: Only 20% of Vermonters approve of President Trump, the lowest in New England. Democrats are more engaged: 69% say they’re extremely interested in the election, compared with 59% of Republicans. Janoo is better liked than Scott, with 54% favorable to his 42%. 38% of Janoo’s supporters say they voted for Scott in 2024. That’s reported crossover, the kind of shift a challenger needs. Read in full, the UNH poll measures a close race two ways, and the two point in different directions: whom voters support, and whom they expect to win. The release’s presentation leans further than its numbers do, with a “blue wave” headline the survey doesn’t establish and a September chart labeled with leaners it didn’t have. “A poll in the homestretch isn’t what tells us we’re succeeding,” Janoo said in Monday’s release. She pointed instead to turnout at her campaign’s canvasses and its endorsements, and said the campaign would spend every second until the polls close getting out the vote. Scott’s campaign has argued that polls understate his support. After the September polls, spokesperson Emma Shouldice said that “public polling has always undervalued the Governor’s support.” As of Friday, nearly 140,000 Vermonters had already voted, according to the Secretary of State’s office. That’s nearly half the 292,000 ballots cast in Vermont’s 2022 general election. Polls are open until 7 p.m. Tuesday. News comes from the facts. Opinions should only come from you. title: NH Democrats expand leads in final UNH poll before Election Day 2026 - Seacoastonline.com
content: Democrats have opened leads in the races for U.S. Senate and New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District in the final days before the election, according to the latest University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll. The poll, released Nov. 1, found Rep. Chris Pappas, D-NH, expanding his lead over former Sen. John E. Sununu, R-NH, in the race for U.S. Senate by four points. Former Portsmouth city councilor Stefany Shaheen, a Democrat, has expanded her lead over Republican businessman Anthony DiLorenzo by nine points. The poll also found the race for governor between Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington narrowing to a tie, although the poll notes most voters think Ayotte will win. The survey comes as polls across the country have found Democrats in the lead and pundits speculate about a “blue wave.” The president’s party typically loses seats in midterm elections. The poll surveyed 2,182 New Hampshire residents online from Oct. 27-31. It has a margin of error of +/-2.1%. In the final days of the election, the poll found Pappas leading Sununu 54% to 42%, up from 50% to 42% in September. It also found that while Pappas’s net favorability of -6 stayed the same since September, Sununu’s has declined from -5 to -18, with notable declines among Independents and Democrats. The drop is likely due to negative campaigning in the final weeks of the campaign, the poll said. Much of Pappas’s negative campaigning against Sununu has been connecting him to President Donald Trump. Sununu has sought to distance himself from the president but had received his endorsement earlier this year. The poll revealed that of Pappas supporters, 87% say their vote is to oppose Trump. “The Democratic Party has done an effective job making this election a referendum on President Trump,” the poll said. The House races also see Democratic leads: while Shaheen in September only had a four point lead over DiLorenzo, she now leads him 56% to 43%. Rep. Maggie Goodlander, D-NH, has maintained a double-digit lead over her Republican challenger, Lily Tang Williams, 56%-41%. The governor’s race between Ayotte and Warmington has “tightened significantly in the past month,” the poll revealed. While Ayotte led Warmington 47%-43% in September, the poll this month found them locked at 48% each. Warmington’s increase in support came from Democrats coalescing around her: 92% of Democrats now say they support Warmington, up from 83% in September. Despite the closeness of the polls, 75% of Granite Staters think that Ayotte will win, including 59% of Democrats. But in the New Hampshire legislature, Democrats hold leads on the generic ballot for Executive Council, state Senate and state House; all leads that have grown since September. Over half (53%) of voters say they plan to vote for a Democrat for Executive Council, 54% say they plan to vote for a Democrat for state Senate and 51% say they plan to vote Democrat for state House. Due to the gerrymandering of the state legislature seats, poll director Andrew Smith said that Democrats generally have to win 54% of the vote to take the majority in the state Senate. Republicans currently control the Executive Council 4-1, the state House 211-170 and the Senate 16-8.

content:
Democratic/Progressive gubernatorial candidate Amanda Janoo has an 8-point lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Phil Scott, according to the final poll of the campaign released on Sunday by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center. Conducted online between October 27 and 31, the Green Mountain State Poll surveyed 1,231 respondents. Of likely voters, 51 percent said they will or have voted for Janoo, while 43 percent say they will or have voted for Scott. The results include participants who said they are leaning toward a candidate, a category not included in previous UNH surveys. The poll’s margin of error is 2.8 percent. Independent Brian Judd received support from 4 percent of survey participants. One percent said they support Freedom and Unity candidate Dean Roy, a high school student. Fewer than one percent said they would vote for June Goodband, the Peace and Justice candidate. Despite the results, the survey found that 62 percent of likely voters believe that Scott will win the election. Only 25 percent of voters think Janoo will win, and 13 percent are unsure. Janoo is more personally popular than Scott, the survey found. Fifty-four percent of likely voters have a favorable opinion of the 39-year-old political newcomer, compared to 42 percent who have a favorable opinion of the governor. Among likely voters who identify as Democrats, 78 percent support Janoo and 20 percent support Scott. Among Republicans, 85 percent support Scott and 10 percent support Judd, the independent candidate, the survey found. An earlier poll from UNH, released in late September, showed that 49 percent of likely voters backed Janoo, compared with 43 percent for Scott. But a poll released by Vermont Public soon after had Scott up 10 points. The Vermont Public poll found that 16 percent of voters were still undecided. A State Navigate poll, released on October 27, showed Scott with a 3-point lead over Janoo. Sixty-six percent of likely voters, including those leaning toward a candidate, said they will or have voted for Balint while 31 percent said they will or have voted for Malloy. title: New poll shows Janoo ahead of Scott in Vermont governor’s race - WCAX
content:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - The final poll before Election Day shows Amanda Janoo ahead of Phil Scott in Vermont’s race for governor. Of likely voters polled, 51% say they have or will vote for Janoo, while 43% want Scott to return for a record-setting sixth term. Just over 1,200 people took part in the poll, which was conducted by the UNH Survey Center. “All the indications are that Amanda Janoo has run an effective campaign,” said Matt Dickinson, a Middlebury College political science professor. Dickinson said the new UNH polling numbers reveal just how close this contest could be between political newcomer Janoo and the incumbent Scott. If the Democrat pulls off the win, it would be historic. “We haven’t seen an incumbent governor defeated since 1962,” Dickinson said. The poll shows affordability and high taxes are top concerns for Vermonters. They are two issues Scott has campaigned on and made his top priorities for years. But Dickinson said the Republican’s time in office could be partly the reason Janoo pulled ahead by 8 points. “Voters don’t feel they’ve been solved,” Dickinson said. “The finger is getting pointed at Phil Scott. At least according to the polls, enough voters are considering an alternative in that top spot.” But Scott, commonly named the most popular governor in the country, still gets high marks here. “His approval ratings in this poll are still quite high. title: Monday Memo: UNH Says Gov Race Tied. Campaign Pros Say ‘Meh.’ - NH Journal
content: The Monday Memo is a mix of reporting, rumors, analysis, and unkind comments compiled from various sources and provided for your entertainment and enlightenment each Monday. Reader discretion is advised. Surprised by UNH Survey Showing Tied Gov’s Race? Don’t Be. Like the swallows returning to Capistrano, or new revelations of antisemitic statements by Abdul El-Sayed, so it is with the last-minute University of New Hampshire Survey Center dump of a “poll” that gets lots of headlines before the election and is quickly forgotten afterward. According to the UNH Survey Center, with just a day to go in the campaign, the New Hampshire governor’s race is tied at 48% each for Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington. This shocking result sent a shockwave through the state’s political circles. The survey also found former U.S. Sen. John Sununu losing to future U.S. Senator Chris Pappas by double digits at 54% to 42%. The survey found a similar margin in the NH-01 race (Shaheen 56%, DiLorenzo 43%). “Because it’s garbage,” one GOP campaign operative told NHJournal. The RealClearPolitics polling average has Ayotte leading the race by nearly nine points. Warmington has never led — or even been close — in the polling average. If Team Ayotte isn’t losing sleep over these numbers, perhaps it’s because the Democratic Governors Association still hasn’t acknowledged that Warmington’s even running. Or because the DGA has yet to give her a single dollar of support, which is why the current spate of TV ads is being paid for out of Warmington’s own pocket. Or maybe it’s because they remember the final UNH Survey of 2024: “Ayotte Holds Small Lead Over Craig in NH Governor’s Race.” That survey had Ayotte and former Manchester Mayor Joyce Craig in a margin-of-error race (Ayotte 48, Craig 44). The final result? Ayotte won by more than nine points. In 2022, it was “Senate & CD1 Too Close to Call in NH.” Sen. Maggie Hassan barely beat Republican Don Bolduc, 50% to 48%, while Rep. Chris Pappas fought for his political life against Karoline Leavitt, 50% to 49%; at least, according to UNH. Final number: Pappas won by eight and Hassan won by nine. And again in 2018: “NH Governor Race Too Close To Call,” with Chris Sununu and former state Sen. Molly Kelly tied at 46%. Final answer? Sununu by seven. UNH has also gotten some races pretty close, to be fair. They predicted big wins for Reps. Kuster and Pappas in 2018, and had Sununu way ahead in 2020 and 2022. Then again, an average Concord barroom drunk could have done the same. The point is, while the UNH number will get lots of clicks and plenty of press, New Hampshire campaign pros are shrugging it off. Dr. Smith’s survey operation may not be a Dartmouth College disaster (it had Craig leading Ayotte by 17 points in 2024), but its numbers aren’t enough to keep candidates up at night, either. Bow and arrow? Check. Horseback? Check. “Free Palestine?” Check. Rep. Ellen Read is a lock for reelection as a Newmarket state rep. Hey, how many of the other 399 could even get on a horse? Much less go full “Pocahontas” from the saddle? Why the horse, you ask? What does that have to do with serving as a state rep? You could ask the same question about “Free Palestine.” Some mean-spirited Republicans have suggested she’s on horseback because the courts have taken away her driving privileges, and she’ll soon be riding Seabiscuit to the State House. Not a chance. That’s the question Rep. Joe Sweeney, R-Salem, is asking about a series of mailers without the “paid for” disclaimers that are required by federal and state law that hit mailboxes last week. The mailers, which were sent by a Democratic print shop in Massachusetts, attack Republican John Sununu and boost third-party candidate Edmond Laplante. The attorney general has sent a cease-and-desist letter to the Journeyman Press and Pinpoint Campaigns, the two businesses responsible for the mailer. According to Sweeney, “the New Hampshire Democratic Party’s own campaign finance report shows the party paid (Pinpoint Campaigns) $58,437.43 for ‘Mailing Services’ this month.” He also says “Journeyman Press has taken 91 payments from New Hampshire Democratic committees and candidates since 2024.” Sweeney has posted these questions for the state Democratic Party and Chairman Ray Buckley: “Democrats are so desperate to stop John Sununu that they’re taking a page out of Mary Peltola’s book and trying to rig the election,” says the NRSC. If this story sounds familiar, it should. During the 2022 GOP primary in the 2nd Congressional District, illegal mail poured in to boost Bob Burns over popular Keene Mayor George Hansel. The mail was eventually traced back to the Democrats’ House Majority PAC in Washington, D.C. Several NHJournal readers have sent screen captures of this ad, which has popped up on their computer screens. Obviously it’s the wrong Sununu, but that’s not unusual. Hardly a day goes by when some national news anchor or debate moderator isn’t calling John “Chris.” Given the younger Sununu’s recent tenure as a popular four-term governor, and the 18 years since John last ran for public office, it’s an inevitable slip of the tongue. But what’s the deal with this ad? It’s been around for weeks, and it’s never been corrected. NHJournal would contact the alleged sponsors, the “Independence Project,” but they don’t exist. Go to the “Independence Project” website, and it’s a single, static image. No contact information, no explanation of why they’re running political ads. Maybe it’s just to annoy John E. Sununu, who is clearly bugged by the “Sunu-who?” issue. The NYTimes reports that Democrats have internal polling on the issue and “they say confusion abounds.” Chris Sununu has already given his answer. “Look, if people thought they were voting for me, my brother would be up by 30 points. Come on.” The New York Times reported last week that Alaska U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola knew about the conspiracy to find someone named Dan Sullivan and get him on the ballot to confuse voters hoping to vote for incumbent GOP U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan. That report has been confirmed by multiple sources, not least of which is that “Decoy Dan” has fled his home in the wake of the revelations. While Peltola may be running on the other side of the continent, the Alaska congresswoman has a close connection to New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas — close enough that they’ve sent joint fundraising emails. Now that Peltola’s been exposed for participating in this high-profile dirty trick, one designed to defraud voters, does Pappas still endorse her for U.S. Senate? Pappas declined to respond to multiple requests for comment after The New York Times reporting. Interestingly, Pappas also declined to respond when Graham Platner was his party’s nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine. Despite his Nazi tattoo, his anti-gay slurs, and credible charges of abusing women, Pappas would not condemn Platner’s statements or behavior until after it was clear the offensive oysterman was going to be off the ballot. Compare that to what Pappas’s fellow congressional Democrat, Haley Stevens, is doing in Michigan, standing up against the antisemitic, pro-Hamas U.S. Senate nominee of her own party. title: Why You're More Likely to Hit a Deer After the Clocks Fall Back - University of New Hampshire
content: Why do deer collisions increase in the fall, especially when daylight savings time ends? As UNH professor Remington Moll explains above, drivers across New England should be extra cautious as the clocks fall back and evening commutes suddenly take place in the dark. The end of daylight savings time coincides with peak deer mating season, when deer — particularly male deer — become more active as they search for mates. With more deer moving around and reduced visibility during evening commutes, the risk of deer-vehicle collisions increases. As you drive this fall, especially after sunset, stay alert, watch for deer near roadways, and remember that if you see one deer, others may be nearby. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Voices of UNH Manchester Wildcats Series: Meet Mechanical Engineering Technology Major, Kieran McCurdy, '25 - University of New Hampshire

For Kieran, the decision to attend UNH Manchester was driven by the program’s practical focus and its strong industry connections. He shares, “UNH Manchester is a hub for all these different companies. When you graduate, there are all these job opportunities that you can go into.” The campus’s location in the heart of Manchester, NH, puts students close to leading engineering firms and tech companies, opening doors to internships, networking, and career placement right after graduation. Kieran’s experience in the mechanical engineering technology program is marked by a diverse curriculum and hands-on learning. He explains, “My favorite thing about the mechanical engineering technology program at UNH Manchester is the array of classes you take. Classes at UNH Manchester teach students not only theory; they also show them how to apply their knowledge in real-world situations. Kieran notes, “I’m taking a 3D printing class. With this class, I’ve been able to level up my 3D printing skills because I’m able to think more critically about the way I design.” The program’s modern facilities, including advanced labs and equipment, further support this hands-on approach. You’re required to make three 3D printed parts per robot and three machine parts per robot.” The project culminates in a friendly competition that lets students test their creations and celebrate their achievements. This experience encourages teamwork, critical thinking, and practical problem-solving. Kieran’s time at UNH Manchester has been filled with opportunities to apply his skills in real-world settings. title: Dems Hold Leads in Exec. Council, NH Senate, NH House and Federal Races; Governor's Race Deadlocked: Final 2026 UNH Poll - InDepthNH.org
content:
InDepthNH.org (https://indepthnh.org/2026/11/01/dems-hold-leads-in-exec-council-nh-senate-nh-house-and-federal-races-governors-race-deadlocked-final-2026-unh-poll/) Gov. Kelly Ayotte is pictured at left and candidate Cinde Warmington at right. Democrats hold leads in the races for Executive Council, the State Senate, and State House and are generally more interested in the election. Affordability or inflation are the most important issues in the election to likely voters, according to the last election poll for 2026 by UNH Survey Center released Sunday night by Andrew Smith Ph.D.. With the election campaign nearly over, Democrat Chris Pappas continues to lead Republican John E. Sununu in the race for U.S. Senate in New Hampshire. Incumbent Democrat Maggie Goodlander holds a comfortable lead over Republican nominee Lily Tang Williams in New Hampshire’s Second Congressional District, while Democrat Stefany Shaheen holds a lead over Republican Anthony DiLorenzo in CD1. Incumbent Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte is statistically tied with Democrat Cinde Warmington, but Ayotte is the more personally popular of the two and most expect her to win re-election, according to the poll. For complete press release and detailed tabular results, please click: These findings are based on the latest Granite State Poll, conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center. Granite State Panel members were sent an invitation to complete the survey and 1,857 completed the survey online. In addition, 325 New Hampshire residents completed the survey after receiving an invitation via text message to complete the survey. Overall, 2,182 New Hampshire residents completed the survey online between October 27 and October 31, 2026. The margin of sampling error for the survey is +/- 2.1 percent. Included in the sample were 2,040 likely general election voters (margin of sampling error +/- 2.2 percent), 1,032 of whom reside in New Hampshire’s First Congressional District (MOE +/- 3.1 percent) and 1,005 of whom reside in New Hampshire’s Second Congressional District (MOE +/- 3.1 percent). By KATHARINE WEBSTER, InDepthNH.org



Turning Point Action, part of the movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk to energize young conservatives, got plenty of media attention on Election Day for bringing celebrities to New Hampshire polling places – and for an alleged assault by a 70-year-old on one of the group’s representatives in Laconia. By PAULA TRACY, InDepthNH.org



CONCORD - The state has never had an all-Democratic Executive Council, but it appears from unofficial vote tallies that it will have one for the next two years after voters turned out and turned down re-election bids for four seats held by Republicans, Tuesday."This election marks an extraordinary new chapter for New Hampshire," said Executive Councilor Karen Liot Hill, D-Lebanon, the lone Democrat currently on the five-member council who won re-election.The council approves all state contracts over $10,000 and the governor's nominations.In a telephone interview, Wednesday she said she did not consider a scenario where it would be all Democrats on the council and was surprised by the vote.She noted it comes with "tremendous responsibility...voters' expectations are going to be high so it's going to be a challenge."Liot Hill is finishing her first term on the council."After two years as the only Democrat on the Executive Council, I’m thrilled to welcome four new colleagues to the table, and I take seriously the responsibility that comes with this new majority."At both the state and federal levels, voters have changed the balance of power, reaffirming the importance of checks and balances in our democracy. By DAMIEN FISHER, InDepthNH.org



Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s agenda for the next two years is taking a back seat to Democrats, who now have veto-proof control in the House and Senate. InDepthNH.org is republishing this Associated Press story in partnership with the AP Journalism Fund

BOSTON (WHDH) - Election Day is Tuesday and voters are set to voice their choice and in four of the biggest races we’re watching, we are seeing three candidates with big leads and one race that’s in a dead heat, according to our Exclusive 7NEWS/University of New Hampshire poll. In the race for governor in Massachusetts, Democrat Mauray Healey is looking to win another term against Republican challenger MIke Minogue. In our poll, Healey holds 55 percent of the vote, with Minogue getting 36 percent. Independent candidate Ashley James grabbed 4 percent. UNH Survey Center Director Andy Smith said President Trump is having a big impact on the race. “We’re seeing on our elections polling, not just in Massachusetts but across New England, is that Democratic voters are really excited and looking forward to going out to vote and every one of their votes is essentially a vote against Donald Trump. It’s going to be very difficult for him to peel off some of those voters,” he said. In the Massachusetts U.S. Senate race, Sen. Ed Markey leads attorney John Deaton by 21 points. We also polled likely voters in the Granite State about who they’re supporting in the New Hampshire U.S. Senate race. U.S. Congressman and Democrate Chris Pappas leads Republican and former Senator John Sununu by 12 points, 54 to 42 percent. The tightest race in our poll is the race for governor in New Hampshire, where incumbent Republican Kelly Ayotte and challenger Democrat and attorney Ciny Warmington are at dead heat at 48 percent. Software developer Stephen Villee grabbed 2 percent of support. “It’s not really a race between Ayotte and Warmington … it’s really a race where the Democrats are going to come out and vote in that Senate race and they’re going to vote Democrat down that ticket,” he said.
